stories.headline: Google DeepMind unveils Genie 4, a world model that simulates scenes with native sound, speech, and physics
stories.why_read: The biggest AI story on Hacker News overnight, and world models are the training ground for the robots and agents you keep reposting about.
body: Google DeepMind announced Genie 4, a new generation of its world model for real-time, interactive world simulation. It is natively multimodal, generating audio alongside the simulated world, and DeepMind says it builds on its Gemini models, including Gemini Omni.

World models like this are a training ground for robots and agents, which is why the launch matters beyond the demos. Genie 4 is rolling out first as a research preview for trusted testers, then to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and to Gemini API partners. The post drew more than 900 points and over 500 comments on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Cybercabs now outnumber Model Ys in Tesla's Texas robotaxi fleet: 573 to 507
stories.why_read: The Cybercab ramp just crossed over in the DMV data, and last night you reposted Damon Hill's first Cybercab ride and the 2,402 percent growth chart.
body: X's news summary of recent Texas data says Tesla's robotaxi fleet in the state has passed 1,000 vehicles, with 573 Cybercabs now outnumbering 507 Model Ys after nearly 200 vehicles were added in a week. Validation units have been seen on Dallas roads, and Musk has mentioned Florida beach areas as a next step.

The posts you reposted fill in the mood: 1996 Formula 1 champion Damon Hill took his first Cybercab ride in Austin, @nishkidoonoo shared a tracker chart showing robotaxi growth of 2,402 percent since May 27, and @nymbusjp set next month's fleet target at 2,000 vehicles, saying 1,800 would do. In Houston, where the service area just grew about tenfold, the police officers' union is urging people to use robotaxis.

stories.headline: Anthropic reports early progress using Claude across real drug programs, including its own muscular dystrophy work
stories.why_read: A concrete look at AI doing science across a whole pipeline, not just molecule design, from the company whose S-1 everyone dissected yesterday.
body: Anthropic's life sciences team says it has spent months in research partnerships with six drug developers: BigHat Biosciences, Bristol Myers Squibb, Divergence Labs, Enveda, Generate Biomedicines, and The Column Group. It has also started discovery programs of its own, including work on rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy.

The post covers how Claude is being used inside these partner programs and Anthropic's own, and the company frames it as early progress it plans to build on. On Hacker News it drew more than 230 points and a comment thread just as long.

stories.headline: The classification of finite simple groups is now fully formalized in Lean, and it turned up a flaw in a published proof
stories.why_read: Squarely in your pinned math interest: one of the largest proofs ever written, now checked line by line by a machine.
body: A team at Axiom Math has published a complete Lean formalization of the classification of finite simple groups, following the first-generation proof, with every logical step checked by Lean's kernel. That proof spans thousands of journal pages by about a hundred mathematicians, and it says every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating, of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups.

Along the way, the team found counterexamples to a closure claim used in a published route to the Unbalanced Group Theorem, and wrote a separate paper with an alternative argument for the simple-group case. They say they're compiling the errata they found with group theorists.

stories.headline: SpaceX tells the FAA it wants to launch 10,000 times a year
stories.why_read: You reposted it last night, and the number reframes airspace and spaceport planning for the next decade.
body: According to the post by @xdNiBoR that you reposted, SpaceX said in a comment to the FAA that it wants to launch 10,000 times a year, as the agency prepares for 10,000 launches a year by 2035.

Separately, @aaronburnett noted that SpaceX is hiring for a Starbase supercomputer after acquiring 444 acres, and @Vol888 reported that Morgan Stanley raised its SpaceX price target to $300 after earnings, the highest on the Street.

stories.headline: A 9.5-severity flaw in UEFI reference firmware threatens most of the world's servers
stories.why_read: Boot-level code execution in the firmware almost every server vendor ships; worth knowing before your infra teams ask.
body: Ars Technica reports a memory-corruption bug, CVE-2026-97631, in an ICMP component of TianoCore EDK II, the open source codebase nearly every UEFI supplier uses, including AMI, Insyde, Phoenix, and Microsoft's hardened Project Mu fork. Exploiting it lets attackers run code before the operating system and before defenses like Secure Boot take hold.

The payload itself doesn't persist, but it opens a door to install payloads that do. The flaw was found by Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google, who had planned a coordinated disclosure in January before it surfaced early.

stories.headline: Inside Tesla's Optimus "robot university": 24-pound camera suits, three shifts, around the clock
stories.why_read: You reposted Scoble's leak, and it explains where Optimus's training data will come from.
body: Robert Scoble posted that workers at Tesla's Palo Alto facility are running a "robot university", wearing 24-pound suits with up to 40 cameras plus 3D sensors to capture what they do. He says they work three shifts, 24 hours a day, that similar efforts have been seen in Texas, and that separate teams record home tasks and factory tasks.

It lands next to a lighter exchange you also saw: John Carmack's reality check that no robot can yet change the batteries in a jack-o-lantern, Musk's reply invoking a Swiss watch and a baseball, and @DirtyTesLa's plea to just see robots fold laundry.

stories.headline: Ghostty 1.4 ships: big speed and memory gains, and complete Kitty graphics support
stories.why_read: The top Hacker News post this morning, and a terminal upgrade worth taking for the security fixes alone.
body: Ghostty 1.4.0 is a major release built from seven months of work, 172 contributors, and 2,889 commits. It brings large performance and memory improvements, SSH integration upgrades, and a 100 percent complete Kitty graphics implementation, which the maintainers say makes Ghostty the first terminal other than Kitty to get there.
The release also includes security fixes, including to paste protection and to Kitty graphics handling. It passed 1,000 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Python's experimental JIT compiler is on its way out
stories.why_read: A rare reversal on a headline CPython feature, and a case study in how big features land, or don't, in open source.
body: LWN reports that CPython's experimental JIT, added for Python 3.13 by Brandt Bucher, appears to be on its way out. The steering council paused the work in June pending a PEP, and the maintainers have now withdrawn PEP 836, nicknamed "JIT Go Brrr". It drew more than 500 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Tailscale discloses privilege-escalation bugs in Tailscale SSH and readies a patch
stories.why_read: If your homelab or work boxes use Tailscale SSH, check your configuration and watch for the update.
body: Tailscale says it's investigating privilege-escalation vulnerabilities in Tailscale SSH. It isn't recommending everyone disable the feature, and it was targeting fixes by the end of Tuesday, October 27, so it's worth checking for the patched client.

stories.headline: Liquid AI releases LFM3, open-weight models that cover text, vision, audio, and more in about 2B parameters
stories.why_read: Small, open, fine-tunable models built for agentic work on a laptop or a Raspberry Pi, right in your open-source LLM lane.
body: Liquid AI's LFM3 family puts text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models on one shared backbone trained on 22 trillion tokens, with the first release in the 2B range. The company says it used hardware-in-the-loop architecture search across 14 device and backend combinations, from phones to a Raspberry Pi 5 to Apple and AMD laptops. X's summary describes six open-weight models with a 256K context window that fit in about 1 GB at 4-bit; weights are on Hugging Face.

stories.headline: Survival LLM: an offline AI assistant with an emergency library that runs on your own computer
stories.why_read: A thoughtful, practical use of local models, with sources shown for every answer.
body: Survival LLM is a free, open source app that answers questions like keeping food safe in a blackout or treating a burn from a local library of medical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, repair guides, and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles. Nothing leaves the machine, every answer lists the articles it used, and the app picks a model size to fit your memory. It runs on Apple Silicon Macs and 64-bit Windows, and it hit the Hacker News front page with more than 370 points.

stories.headline: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash leads real-world usage on OpenRouter
stories.why_read: Open weights winning on actual token volume, not just benchmarks, which is the cost story behind your agent bills.
body: X's news summary says DeepSeek V4.1 Flash now tops OpenRouter usage. Users cite costs 13 to 20 times lower than top closed models, and an abliterated variant is reported to run 2.7 times faster with 40 percent fewer reasoning tokens.

stories.headline: RudderStack open-sources DevBox, the agent that now merges about 35 percent of its internal PRs
stories.why_read: You reposted the launch; it's a self-hosted, org-wide coding agent that works from Linear tickets, close to how your bot fleet already works.
body: RudderStack released DevBox under the MIT license. You hand it a ticket and it plans the change, writes code, runs tests, reviews its own work, and opens a draft pull request; comments on the PR send it back to push fixes. It runs on your own infrastructure with your model keys, and the README says it merges about 35 percent of RudderStack's internal pull requests with roughly an 80 percent merge rate.

stories.headline: Grok Bot routines can now fire from webhooks, and Cursor says it's starting to hire bots onto its team
stories.why_read: Both posts are in last night's bookmarks, and webhooks are a direct upgrade for your own bot routines.
body: @melvindvivas walked through Grok Bot webhooks: create a routine with a webhook trigger, then call its POST URL with the authorization header from any outside app. In the same feed, Cursor's @mntruell posted that the company is beginning to hire bots onto its team.
X's news roundup also has users weighing whether Grok Bot's $30-a-month plan is worth it.

stories.headline: What do you call the tasks agents are great at? Developers argue over "verifiable" and "grindable"
stories.why_read: A useful lens for deciding which of your tasks to hand to agents outright.
body: Matt Pocock asked for a word for tasks where an agent can verify its own work and hill-climb toward the answer, the kind you can hand off and let it grind.
Theo's post asking whether @poteto really burns $132 million a year in tokens, which you reposted, makes the other half of the case: "No. But if she did, it would be worth it."

stories.headline: Meta falls about 20 percent as it plans up to $97.5 billion in stock sales to fund AI, with Nvidia investing $3 billion
stories.why_read: A huge signal about what AI capex is now costing even the richest companies, and Nvidia is on both sides of it.
body: According to X's news summary, Meta reported third-quarter revenue up 26 percent to $64.6 billion, but the stock fell about 20 percent as investors focused on 2026 capital spending of $135 to $145 billion and a plan to raise up to $97.5 billion through stock sales, starting with $35 billion at about $625 a share. Nvidia is investing $3 billion, and AMD up to $5 billion.

stories.headline: General Compute raises $100M to run fast inference on non-Nvidia chips in old Bitcoin mines
stories.why_read: An inference bet built on SambaNova, Cerebras, and Positron hardware rather than GPUs.
body: X's summary says General Compute's $100 million Series A took its valuation from $60 million to $800 million in five months, alongside $400 million in debt. It runs inference on SambaNova, Cerebras, and Positron hardware and is converting Bitcoin mines into data centers.

stories.headline: Why Micron is skipping 4F² DRAM, as Nvidia and Micron make up a third of the US earnings boom
stories.why_read: Memory is the quiet bottleneck behind every GPU story, and these two pieces explain the engineering and the money.
body: HotHardware explains the DRAM cell-geometry race: memory has long used a 6F² layout, the next goal is denser 4F² cells, and Micron is suddenly backing away from 4F² while rivals double down. Its expanded Boise campus will produce 1-delta memory.
On the money side, a Wall Street Journal analysis that hit Hacker News finds that Nvidia and Micron alone account for 34 percent of America's earnings growth, a sign of how narrow the boom is.

stories.headline: A new engineering benchmark finds the best AI model passes only 37 percent of real design tasks
stories.why_read: A sober read on how far models still are from real engineering design work.
body: Xplore AI's Real World Engineering Bench tests 11 models on 20 engineering tasks. X's summary says GPT-6 Astra leads at 37 percent and Claude Opus 5.5 follows at 29 percent.

stories.headline: More than 1,000 mathematicians join a group that rejects AI in research
stories.why_read: The flip side of the Lean formalization story, and a real split forming in your favorite science.
body: X's news summary says the Association for Human Mathematics now has more than 1,000 members, including 654 in an AI-free caucus. It formed partly as a reaction to OpenAI's 722 AI-generated math manuscripts.

stories.headline: Infisical raises $40M for Agent Vault, which hands AI agents fake keys
stories.why_read: A clean pattern for keeping credentials away from agents, which matters for any bot fleet with real access.
body: X's summary says Infisical raised a $40 million Series B at a $600 million valuation, led by Elad Gil. Its Agent Vault gives agents fake keys and swaps in real ones through a proxy. More than 1,300 organizations use Infisical, and it secures 10 billion secrets a day.

stories.headline: Back-of-envelope math puts Tesla's robotaxi at about 8 percent of Austin's rideshare market
stories.why_read: A rough but grounded way to think about how far the Austin fleet still has to grow, from a post you reposted.
body: @TSLAFanMtl estimates Austin needs about 10,000 cars to cover its whole rideshare market, or about 240,000 rider hours. With about 1,051 vehicles running 19 hours a day, Tesla is at roughly 20,000 rider hours, or about 8 percent share by this math.

stories.headline: Palmer Luckey unveils BlueChip, billed as the first American-built computer in decades
stories.why_read: A hardware-sovereignty story that sits next to The Grid PCB factory you bookmarked earlier this week.
body: Palmer Luckey posted BlueChip, which he calls the first American computer in decades, designed in California and built in America.

stories.headline: Apple launches the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6, pitched for running LLMs locally
stories.why_read: If you run local models on a Mac, the AI throughput numbers are the part to read.
body: Apple says M6 has a 12-core CPU and a 12-core GPU with up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads than M5, plus more Neural Accelerators in the GPU and what it calls a dual 16-core Neural Engine. The new MacBook Pro adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 and is rated for up to 24 hours of battery. A new iMac with M6 also hit the Hacker News front page.

stories.headline: A Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Pi 4 Model A show up in kernel device trees
stories.why_read: A big compute jump for the Zero line, spotted in Linux source before any announcement.
body: Bret.dk spotted a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Pi 4 Model A in new device tree files. The Zero 3 W appears to use the BCM2711, the quad-core Cortex-A72 chip from the Pi 4, about five years after the Zero 2 W launched. There's no official announcement yet.

stories.headline: Git for the US Code: tracing every line of federal law back to the law that wrote it
stories.why_read: Version control applied to statutes, with a clear argument for why LLM legal research needs it.
body: Lexifina makes the case that lawyers should be able to see who wrote any line of a statute and when, the way programmers use git blame. Its worked example is the small business debtor limit in 11 USC 1182(1), now $3,424,000. It drew nearly 300 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: Austin's airport just had its busiest day ever: 46,963 people through TSA
stories.why_read: Home-town news you reposted.
body: Austin-Bergstrom International Airport said TSA screened 46,963 people on Monday, October 26, 2026, the busiest day in the airport's history.

stories.headline: Ink droplets frozen mid-air win the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
stories.why_read: Physics, chemistry, and a self-taught photographer's ingenuity in one image.
body: Ole Bielfeldt, a 25-year-old German photographer, won Nikon's 2026 Small World photomicrography competition against 1,802 entries from 69 countries with an image of inkjet droplets. He learned on a microscope from the attic during COVID, and he doesn't use AI in his images.

stories.headline: Diwali at Costco
stories.why_read: A little festive joy from your reposts, for the season.
body: @DcWalaDesi shared Diwali at Costco, a small, cheerful sign of the season in American aisles. You reposted it last night.
